liturgical_day: Tuesday of the Twenty-first Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: The weight of mercy
theme: Jesus exposes a religion that measures herbs precisely while neglecting judgment, mercy, and faith. He does not oppose careful obedience; he restores its true order, calling for an inner cleansing from which outward integrity can grow.
introduction: In the Temple courts, Jesus turns from distorted rules about oaths to the deeper distortion beneath them. The scribes and Pharisees can count out the smallest garden herbs for tithing, yet their precision has become a shelter from the law’s greater demands. Judgment, mercy, and faith are not alternatives to obedience but its heart and weight. Christ therefore refuses two evasions at once: the lesser duties should not be abandoned, and the greater ones must never be displaced by them. His picture of straining a gnat and swallowing a camel makes the disorder impossible to miss. The second woe carries the challenge inward. A polished cup cannot make corrupt contents clean, and a convincing religious appearance cannot purify a conscience filled with grasping and impurity. The Fathers read Christ’s command as a summons to truth before God: clean the heart, order the conscience, and the body’s conduct will follow. Holiness is neither spectacle nor selective exactness. It is the integrity of a life in which visible practice rises from a soul being cleansed by grace.
hero_alt: Jesus confronts scribes and Pharisees beside carefully measured herbs, a cup, and a dish in the Temple court, rendered in Byzantine mosaic, stained glass, gold leaf, and luminous sacred geometry
closing_title: Let the greater things have their weight
closing: Christ does not invite us to become careless about small acts of obedience. He commands us to put them back into the order of love. Precision becomes hypocrisy when it protects us from judgment that is honest, mercy that is costly, and faith that entrusts the whole self to God. The gnat and the camel expose how easily conscience can magnify what is manageable while overlooking what would require conversion. The cup and dish press the matter further: even a faultless exterior cannot cleanse what we willingly harbor within. Begin where Jesus directs. Name one inward disorder without disguise—resentment, grasping, vanity, or the wish to appear righteous—and ask for the grace to surrender it. Then join that prayer to one weightier act: judge a situation truthfully, show mercy where it costs you, or keep faith when no one is watching. The Lord’s rebuke is severe because he desires wholeness. When the inside is cleansed, outward obedience no longer serves appearances; it becomes the visible fruit of a heart turned toward God.

verses.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint, anise, and cumin, yet have left aside the weightier things of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith. These you ought to have done, without leaving the others undone.
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: Exactness in lesser duties cannot excuse neglect of justice, mercy, and faith. Jesus restores proportion without dismissing genuine obedience.
verses.commentary: Jerome recalls that tithes supported the priests and Levites, whose portion was the Lord. The Pharisees concentrated on collecting even the smallest herbs while treating the law’s weightier demands lightly. Their fault was not the careful tithe itself, but a covetous selectivity: they pursued what benefited them and neglected justice in dealings, mercy toward the poor, and faith toward God. Christ therefore orders obedience rather than abolishing it. The lesser practice may remain, but it cannot displace the commands that reveal whether love of God and neighbor truly governs a person’s life.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 23:23–24

verses.text: Blind guides, who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel.
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: The absurd picture reveals a conscience with its scale reversed. It anxiously filters tiny faults while allowing grave duties to pass unnoticed.
verses.commentary: Jerome interprets the camel as the weighty precepts just named—judgment, mercy, and faith—and the gnat as meticulous concern for tithing insignificant herbs. The image is deliberately disproportionate. A guide who strains out the smallest creature yet swallows the largest has lost the ability to distinguish moral weight. Jerome’s point is not that small obligations are worthless, but that religious scruple becomes corrupt when it coexists with carelessness about God’s greater commands. Authentic discernment sees both, gives each its proper place, and refuses to let profitable or visible details conceal failures of justice and love.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 23:23–24

verses.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of robbery and impurity.
verses.author: St Hilary of Poitiers
verses.insight: An immaculate exterior cannot redeem corrupt contents. Visible religion has value only when it expresses a conscience being made pure.
verses.commentary: Hilary says Jesus reproves an ostentatious concern for useless exactness while useful morality is neglected. The inside of a cup is the part from which one actually drinks; if it remains foul, polishing the exterior accomplishes nothing. So the image reaches beyond vessels to the human person. Public conduct and bodily appearance may look ordered, yet they cannot substitute for purity of conscience. Christ exposes the contradiction between a carefully managed exterior and an inward life ruled by grasping and impurity. The needed cleansing begins within, where motives, desires, and decisions stand open before God.
verses.source_label: St Hilary of Poitiers, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 23:25–26

verses.text: Blind Pharisee, first clean the inside of the cup and the dish, so that the outside may also become clean.
verses.author: Origen
verses.insight: Christ calls us to become righteous rather than merely to look righteous. Cleansed thoughts and conscience give outward conduct its integrity.
verses.commentary: Origen hears in this command a lesson about reality and appearance. The person who seeks chiefly to be considered righteous attends to what others can see while neglecting the heart and conscience. The one who truly cleans what is within begins with thoughts, desires, and intentions before God; from that inward renewal, the visible life also becomes clean. Jesus therefore does not set inner and outer holiness against each other. He establishes their proper direction. Outward goodness is meant to be the truthful expression of an inwardly ordered person, not a crafted surface that hides corruption or wins admiration.
verses.source_label: Origen, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 23:25–26
